name: Guardian genius crossword No 169
preamble: Each across clue’s wordplay indicates a repeated letter not required in its solution and each down solution requires a repeated letter, not indicated in its wordplay.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: /T_he future leaders of the Marxist revolution were all estranged by Mao in the end

indicators.note: leaders are the front runners, so each word of the phrase gives up only its opening letter
in the end points to the final letter of the dictator's name
estranged means kept apart, so every one of the leading letters is separated from its neighbour by the inserted letter

blocks.note: the leading letter of this word
the last letter of the Chinese leader's name, used to separate each leader
the leading letter of this word
the same final letter again
the leading letter of this word
the same final letter once more
the leading letter of this word; the four initials together are texting shorthand for the answer

explanation.surface: A prophecy that the coming leaders of a communist uprising would all fall out with Chairman Mao.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives TOMOROW, one R short; as the preamble says for every down, the grid needs a repeated letter the wordplay leaves out, so a second R goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomorrow is used as a noun for the time still to come, the days ahead of us.

clue.text: Go and take a quick look

blocks.note: go in the sense of energy or vigour

explanation.walkthrough: Go gives PEP; the preamble asks every down to double a letter the wordplay gives once, so a second E is added for the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To peep is to glance briefly or furtively, often through a small gap.

clue.text: Charm one with the sound of bells

blocks.note: a is the indefinite article, meaning one
a peal is the ringing of a set of bells

explanation.surface: Someone is enchanted by a chiming peal of church bells.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives APEAL; the preamble's rule for downs adds a second P.
explanation.definitionFit: Appeal is attractiveness or allure, the quality that draws people in, much as charm does.

clue.text: Box for one found to the right of aisle’s opening in theatre

indicators.text: found to the right of aisle’s opening in
indicators.note: we keep only the letters standing to the right of the first letter of aisle where it appears inside the playhouse word

blocks.note: the letters after the A of this word

explanation.surface: Directions to a theatre box seat, just right of where the aisle begins.
explanation.walkthrough: Box looks like a theatre box, but it is the evergreen shrub; the wordplay gives TRE and the preamble's rule for downs doubles the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Box is a kind of evergreen shrub or small tree, so it is an example of one.

clue.text: /T_he Bible describes way this vessel rescued animal

indicators.note: to describe can mean to draw a line around, so the scripture letters go round the road

blocks.note: AV is the Authorised Version of the Bible
Rd is the abbreviation for road
Noah's ark, the vessel that saved the animals in the Bible

explanation.surface: Scripture tells how a boat saved a creature from the Flood.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives ARDVARK; the preamble adds a second A for the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardvark is a burrowing African mammal that feeds on ants and termites.

clue.text: Document’s style supports reproduction

blocks.note: to be for something is to support it
mating is breeding, the act of reproduction

explanation.surface: A paper whose style backs the cause of reproduction, perhaps a biology report.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives FORMATING; the preamble's rule for downs doubles the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Formatting is the layout and visual arrangement of a document's text, its overall presentation.

clue.text: /T_hin coat able to be removed in August

indicators.note: this tells us the word able is to be taken out of the word that follows

blocks.note: august as an adjective means respected and dignified

explanation.surface: A thin coat of paint that can be stripped off during the summer month.
explanation.walkthrough: August is not the month but the adjective for venerable; with able gone it gives VENER, and the preamble doubles the E for the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin layer of fine wood or other material glued over a cheaper surface.

clue.text: Managed to cope with Nick going back to join the army again

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word for nick is written right to left

blocks.note: to nick is to steal
re-up is US slang for re-enlisting

explanation.surface: A soldier coped with a spell in the military prison by re-enlisting.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives BORREUP; the preamble says every across wordplay brings a repeated letter the answer does not use, so one R drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear up is to stay resilient under strain, and its past tense means coped.

clue.text: Argued about when one needs odd characters to leave

indicators.note: when the odd-numbered letters go, only the even ones of the word remain

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
as in the sense of while
taken as written
the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A complaint about having to see off strange people.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives REASONEED; the preamble's rule for acrosses drops the repeated E.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason is to present logical points in a discussion, so reasoned means argued a case.

clue.text: Climax doesn’t end with arrest after leader escapes grasp

indicators.note: a word that does not end has had its final letter cut off
when the leader escapes, the first letter of the word runs away

blocks.note: to come is to reach a climax
to apprehend a suspect is to arrest them

explanation.surface: A thriller whose climax is a botched arrest, the suspect slipping out of the officer's grip.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives COMPPREHEND; the preamble's rule for acrosses removes the repeated P.
explanation.definitionFit: To comprehend is to understand fully, which is what grasp means when used of an idea.

clue.text: Attitude that is displayed by soldiers?

indicators.note: something displayed by others is held up within them, like an exhibit in a frame

blocks.note: soldiers are the men of an army
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A question whether this is the attitude troops show.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives MIEEN; the preamble's rule for acrosses removes the repeated E.
explanation.definitionFit: Mien is a person's bearing or manner, the outward look that shows their mood or disposition.

clue.text: Stampede did this enough to dam river ﬂ owing west

indicators.note: a dam sits across a river, so one word is set inside the other
in an across clue, flowing west means running right to left

blocks.note: ample means plenty, enough
the Dart is a river in Devon

explanation.surface: Cattle in a stampede flattened enough ground to block a westward river.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives TRAMPLEAD, with A in it twice; the preamble's rule for acrosses drops the repeated A.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampeding herd tramples whatever lies in its path, crushing it underfoot, so the verb describes what it did.

clue.text: Location of Emirates Stadium’s entrance let media broadcast

indicators.note: the entrance of a word is its first letter
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
the letters as written

explanation.surface: The press were allowed into the Emirates Stadium, the London home of Arsenal football club.
explanation.walkthrough: Emirates Stadium is Arsenal's ground in London, but the definition takes Emirates alone: the United Arab Emirates. The anagram gives MIDLEEAST, and the preamble doubles the D for a down.
explanation.definitionFit: The United Arab Emirates are a federation of Gulf states in the region called the Middle East.

clue.text: Training ground starts to demoralise latest recruits immediately

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters
ground means milled or crushed, so the letters are broken up and remixed

blocks.note: the initials of these four words

explanation.surface: A training ground where the newest recruits are crushed at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Training ground' reads as one phrase, but ground is the anagram signal. The wordplay gives DRIL and the preamble doubles the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Drill is repetitive military or practical training, such as marching exercises on a parade square.

clue.text: Company does put up rent, subject to a 25% discount

indicators.note: to put someone up is to house them, so one word lodges inside the other
a quarter off a four-letter word means one of its letters is lost

blocks.note: acts as in performs or does
rent is the past tense of rend, so tore

explanation.surface: A firm puts up the rent, but grants a quarter off.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent looks like money for housing; it is the past of rend. The wordplay gives ACTTORS and the preamble's rule for acrosses removes the repeated T.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical company is a troupe of performers, so its members collectively are the players.

clue.text: Did cow essentially eat grass?

indicators.note: essentially points to the essence, the central letter of the short word

blocks.note: the middle letter of the word
weed is slang for cannabis, also known as grass

explanation.surface: A farmyard question about whether a cow grazed.
explanation.walkthrough: Cow is a verb, to intimidate, not the animal. The wordplay gives AWEED and the preamble's rule for acrosses drops one E.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to intimidate them, and to awe someone is to overwhelm them into fearful respect.

clue.text: Drive opens up delicate chip shot at the nineteenth?

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to what is had there, rather than a synonym

indicators.note: opening up the word means splitting it so that something can be inserted

blocks.note: a dink is a soft, delicate lob in golf or tennis
Dr is the abbreviation for drive in addresses

explanation.surface: A golfer's round: a drive, then a soft chip, and finally a visit to the nineteenth.
explanation.walkthrough: Drive and chip shot are golf strokes, but drive is a road. The nineteenth hole is golfers' slang for the clubhouse bar. The wordplay gives DDRINK and the preamble drops one D.
explanation.definitionFit: After a round, golfers retire to the clubhouse bar, jokingly called the nineteenth hole, for a drink.

clue.text: Unlikely to reveal spoilers by rolling credits

indicators.note: rolling means tumbling over, so the letters turn into a new order

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A film fan who keeps the plot secret while the end credits scroll.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram gives DISCRET; the preamble's rule for downs adds a second E.
explanation.definitionFit: A discreet person is careful and tactful about keeping secrets, so they would not give away a plot.

clue.text: Stopping retrograde cell division is futile

indicators.note: stopping in the sense of staying, as a guest stops at a hotel, so the letters lodge within the phrase
retrograde means moving backwards, so the phrase is read from right to left

blocks.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A biologist laments that halting backward cell division is pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed run gives IDLLE; the preamble's rule for acrosses removes the repeated L.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle can mean pointless or without effect, as in idle threats, which is what futile means.

clue.text: Drunk has spoken of close relationship to the drink?

definitions.text: of close relationship to the drink?

blocks.note: lit is slang for drunk
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: A drunk talks of how intimately he's bound to alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is slang for the sea, not alcohol. The wordplay gives LITORAL and the preamble doubles the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Littoral means of or on the shore, the zone lying right beside the sea.

clue.text: Witness does this holding state symbol of justice

indicators.note: holding means gripping on the outside, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: a witness is one who sees
Cal is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A courtroom witness clutching a statue of Justice and her emblem.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives SCALEES; the preamble's rule for acrosses removes the repeated E.
explanation.definitionFit: A balance is the emblem carried by the figure of Justice, representing fair weighing of evidence.

clue.text: One who self-harms is more attractive

blocks.note: the comparative of cute

explanation.surface: A grim claim that someone who hurts themselves becomes better-looking.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives CUTER; the preamble's rule for downs doubles the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutter is a term for a person who deliberately injures their own skin with a blade.

clue.text: Had settled game with it before dispute

indicators.note: the first two pieces are placed ahead of the word for had

blocks.note: a bird that has settled has lit, or alighted
tig is the playground chasing game, also called tag
to have a meal is to eat it, so had can be ate

explanation.surface: Someone who settled a match with a ruling before a row broke out.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives LITTIGATE; the preamble's rule for acrosses drops the repeated T.
explanation.definitionFit: To litigate is to contest a matter in court, taking a disagreement to legal action.

clue.text: Start to develop bite by nipping end oﬀ tie

indicators.note: nipping off the end means snipping away the last letter

blocks.note: to tether is to tie up an animal

explanation.surface: A puppy starts to bite, nipping the end off a necktie.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives TETHE; the preamble's rule for downs adds a second E.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby teethes when its first milk teeth are cutting through, so it begins to have a bite.

clue.text: Viewer’s complaint lambasted set incorporating empty theatricality

indicators.note: something lambasted is beaten up, so its letters are knocked into a new order
an emptied word has lost all its insides, leaving only its two outer letters
incorporating means taking into the body, so the reworked word surrounds the short pair

blocks.note: the letters as written
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A TV viewer complains, slamming a stage set with no real drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The viewer is an eye, not a TV watcher. The wordplay gives STTYE and the preamble's rule for acrosses removes the repeated T.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, an ailment of the eye, the organ that views.

clue.text: Free press I only partially control

indicators.note: only partially means just a piece of the phrase, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: the run of letters from inside the phrase

explanation.surface: A dictator boasts that he only half controls a free press.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden run brings REEPRESSION, with E twice; the preamble's rule for acrosses drops one E.
explanation.definitionFit: Repression is the forcible restraint of people or ideas by an authority, keeping them under control.

clue.text: Queen’s response to fuss possibly upset rector at university

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so in a down clue the letters are read bottom to top

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for rector
up is used for being in residence at a university

explanation.surface: How the monarch might react to a rector's commotion at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen here is a female cat, not the monarch. The wordplay gives PUR and the preamble doubles the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A queen is a female cat, and a cat's contented reply to being stroked is a purr.

clue.text: Talk back to American army unit

definitions.note: American flags that the word is chiefly US usage

blocks.note: the SAS is the Special Air Service, a British special forces regiment

explanation.surface: Someone answers back to a US army detachment.
explanation.walkthrough: American belongs to the definition, marking a US term. The wordplay gives SAS and the preamble doubles the S.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English, to sass someone is to answer them cheekily or with disrespect.

clue.text: Workforce curse about introduction of regulation clothing

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the curse goes around the letter
the introduction of a word is its first letter, the one to be enclosed

blocks.note: the men are the workers
to swear is to curse
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Staff swear about new rules on uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives MENSWEARR; the preamble's rule for acrosses drops the repeated R.
explanation.definitionFit: Menswear is garments designed for men, a category of clothes sold in shops.

clue.text: Soldier mounted stairs, skipping every other one, in pursuit of swimmer

indicators.note: skipping every second step leaves only alternate letters
in pursuit of means coming behind, so this piece follows the fish

blocks.note: huss is a dogfish, sold as rock salmon in British fish shops
the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A soldier climbed the stairs two at a time, chasing a swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives HUSSSAR; the preamble's rule for acrosses drops one S.
explanation.definitionFit: A hussar is a cavalryman of a light horse regiment, a soldier who fights on horseback.
